# Custom resources

Generated from `config/crd/bases/*.yaml` -- the same schema `kubectl explain` and `kubectl apply --validate` read. Five namespaced kinds in `spawnery.cloud/v1alpha1`.

A few fields are Kubernetes' own types, embedded by reference rather than declared in this repository: they appear as a single row naming the type and linking to [the Go package reference for `k8s.io/api/core/v1`](https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/api/core/v1) instead of being expanded here.

- [Network](#network)
- [ServerGroup](#servergroup)
- [ProxyGroup](#proxygroup)
- [Server](#server)
- [ScaleBoost](#scaleboost)

## Network

**Scope:** Namespaced &nbsp;&nbsp; **Plural:** `networks` &nbsp;&nbsp; **Short names:** `mcnet`

Network is the root resource of a Minecraft network.

### What `kubectl get` shows

<thead><tr><th>Column</th><th>Type</th><th>JSONPath</th></tr></thead>

</tbody></table></div>

### spec

NetworkSpec describes one Minecraft network. Exactly one Network may exist per namespace; further ones are rejected with an Accepted=False condition.

One field and not two, because they come from the same plugin and a network that styles one should not have to style the other to match.<br><br>MiniMessage, which both platforms parse -- see the agent&#x27;s own Style for why that rather than the deprecated section-sign codes. <code>$EVENT_MESSAGE</code> is replaced by what the line has to say; everything around it is yours. The token keeps its name because an installation has already written it down.<br><br>**Nothing about this reaches podspec.DesiredServerHash.** It travels in the NetworkState the operator already sends, so changing it rolls no pod and takes effect within a resync interval. A format carried in an environment variable would have been in the pod spec, and re-wording a chat line would have replaced every server on the network.<br><br>A value that MiniMessage cannot parse costs the line, not the agent: the agent falls back to the message alone rather than throwing inside a network callback.</details></td></tr>

### spec

ServerGroupSpec describes a group of Minecraft servers.

<div style="overflow-x: auto;"><table>
<thead><tr><th>Field</th><th>Type</th><th>Required</th><th>Default</th><th>Description</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><code>attributes</code></td><td>map[string]string</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Attributes is what plugins are told about this group. See GroupAttributes: the operator carries it and acts on none of it.<details><summary>more</summary>It shapes no pod and is therefore not in the spec hash a server is replaced on -- the opposite of Env above. Editing it replaces nothing and restarts nothing; the next network picture simply carries the new value, which is what a description of a group should cost.</details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>configOverlay</code></td><td>object</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>ConfigOverlay names a ConfigMap whose keys are configuration files to merge over the rendered defaults — &quot;server.properties&quot;, &quot;paper-global.yml&quot;, &quot;paper-world-defaults.yml&quot; or &quot;velocity.toml&quot;, in the target&#x27;s own dialect.<details><summary>more</summary>paper-world-defaults.yml is the one of those the operator writes only when an overlay names it. Nothing in it is operationally critical, so there is nothing to assert into it, and a file written empty on every start would overwrite whatever the server had filled in for itself. It is also the only route that file has: a mount cannot deliver it, because a mount anywhere under /data/config stops the server writing its own configuration and it never starts. See internal/podspec.ServerConfigDirPath.<br><br>It is a field of its own rather than a reserved name inside mounts, because mounts is documented as raw files for plugins and worlds and a name-based convention is invisible until someone picks that name by accident. It outranks the rendered defaults and is outranked by the operationally critical fields, which nothing can reach.<br><br>A key the receiving program does not declare is refused rather than written. Paper and Velocity both keep their own default for a key they do not read and write the stray one straight back out, so the rendered file goes on looking like the override took while the setting never applies -- which is the failure this refusal exists to prevent. The declared keys are taken from each program&#x27;s own default configuration, so a Paper or Velocity bump can refuse a legitimately new key until that file is captured again. server.properties is the exception: it has no such capture, so a mistyped key there is still only an unused one.</details></td></tr>

Empty is not an error: a plugin then shows the group&#x27;s own name, and it is the plugin that makes that substitution rather than the operator, so that a picture with the field unset and a picture whose operator predates the field read the same.</details></td></tr>

<tr><td><code>env</code></td><td>array</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Env are extra environment variables for the server container, appended to the ones the operator sets. <tr><td><code>mounts[].secret</code></td><td><a href="https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/api/core/v1#SecretVolumeSource">SecretVolumeSource</a> (Kubernetes, not expanded here)</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Secret source.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>mounts[].subPath</code></td><td>string</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>SubPath mounts one file or one subdirectory of the source instead of the whole of it, so that MountPath can be a file.<details><summary>more</summary>Without it, a mount whose path names a file gets a *directory* there -- the source&#x27;s keys as separate files inside it. A server looking for /data/bukkit.yml then finds a directory called bukkit.yml, and what it reports is a parse error rather than anything about a mount. Landing a single file beside the ones the server writes itself is the case this exists for; there is no other way to do it.<br><br>**A ConfigMap or Secret mounted through subPath does not update.** Kubernetes refreshes a projected volume in place, and a subPath mount is a bind of one file out of it that the kubelet does not re-point. Editing the ConfigMap changes nothing in a running pod, and nothing reports that. Without subPath the file does update, eventually and without a restart -- which is a real difference and the reason this is a field somebody opts into rather than something inferred from the path looking like a file. Neither behaviour reaches the pod digest either way, so no edit to a ConfigMap&#x27;s contents rolls anything.</details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>networkRef</code></td><td>object</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>NetworkRef names the Network this group belongs to.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>networkRef.name</code></td><td>string (length &gt;= 1)</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>Name of the referenced object.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>replicas</code></td><td>integer (int32) (&gt;= 0)</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Replicas is the fixed number of persistent servers. Ephemeral groups are sized by scaling instead.<details><summary>more</summary>Lowering it takes the top ordinal whoever is on it. A persistent server is an identity and no other server can take its place, so unlike an ephemeral group -- which shrinks around its players by picking an empty server instead -- this one has no alternative to offer. The players on that ordinal are protected by the ordinary drain and by nothing else: they are moved through the proxies, and anyone still connected when spec.drain.timeoutSeconds passes is disconnected with the pod.<br><br>So if they must not be: empty the ordinal first, or raise spec.drain.timeoutSeconds beforehand so the drain has room to finish. docs/guides/persistent-worlds.md carries why refusing to shrink while anyone is online would not be the better rule.</details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>resources</code></td><td><a href="https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/api/core/v1#ResourceRequirements">ResourceRequirements</a> (Kubernetes, not expanded here)</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Resources overrides Network.spec.defaults.resources.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>scaling</code></td><td>object</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Scaling configures slot-based scaling. Ephemeral only.<details><summary>more</summary>Editing it replaces no server: staleness is a digest over the rendered pod, and nothing here shapes one, so a scaling knob can be tuned during a player spike without a changeover.</details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>scaling.maxReplicas</code></td><td>integer (int32) (&gt;= 1)</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>MaxReplicas caps the number of servers.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>scaling.minReplicas</code></td><td>integer (int32) (&gt;= 0)</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>MinReplicas is the number of servers kept running at all times.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>scaling.scaleDownStabilizationSeconds</code></td><td>integer (int32) (&gt;= 0)</td><td align="center"></td><td><code>300</code></td><td>ScaleDownStabilizationSeconds is how long a server must be empty before it is eligible for scale-down.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>scaling.spareSlots</code></td><td>integer (int32) (&gt;= 0)</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>SpareSlots is the number of free player slots kept available.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>scheduling</code></td><td>object</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Scheduling overrides Network.spec.defaults.scheduling.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>scheduling.affinity</code></td><td><a href="https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/api/core/v1#Affinity">Affinity</a> (Kubernetes, not expanded here)</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Affinity expresses scheduling preferences and constraints.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>scheduling.nodeSelector</code></td><td>map[string]string</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>NodeSelector restricts pods to nodes carrying all these labels.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>scheduling.tolerations</code></td><td><a href="https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/api/core/v1#Toleration">[]Toleration</a> (Kubernetes, not expanded here)</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Tolerations allow pods onto tainted nodes.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>storage</code></td><td>object</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Storage configures the PVC. Persistent and OnDemand only.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>storage.accessModes</code></td><td>array of string</td><td align="center"></td><td><code>[ReadWriteOnce]</code></td><td>AccessModes are immutable once set.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>storage.size</code></td><td>object (pattern <code>^(\+|-)?(([0-9]+(\.[0-9]*)?)|(\.[0-9]+))(([KMGTPE]i)|[numkMGTPE]|([eE](\+|-)?(([0-9]+(\.[0-9]*)?)|(\.[0-9]+))))?$</code>)</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>Size of the volume. May grow, never shrink; actual expansion requires allowVolumeExpansion on the StorageClass.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>storage.storageClassName</code></td><td>string</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>StorageClassName is immutable once set.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>terminationGracePeriodSeconds</code></td><td>integer (int64) (&gt;= 1)</td><td align="center"></td><td><code>60</code></td><td>TerminationGracePeriodSeconds is the time the pod gets to save its world.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>type</code></td><td>string (one of: Ephemeral, Persistent, OnDemand)</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>Type selects ephemeral, persistent or on-demand operation. Immutable.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>update</code></td><td>object</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Update configures the rolling update. Ephemeral only.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>update.maxStaleSeconds</code></td><td>integer (int32) (&gt;= 0)</td><td align="center"></td><td><code>0</code></td><td>MaxStaleSeconds forces an active drain of stale servers after this many seconds. 0 means stale servers are never actively emptied.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>update.maxUnavailable</code></td><td>integer (int32) (&gt;= 1)</td><td align="center"></td><td><code>1</code></td><td>MaxUnavailable is how many servers may be draining or terminating at the same time because of a generation change.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>update.minAvailable</code></td><td>integer (int32) (&gt;= 1)</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>MinAvailable is how many servers must stay joinable while the group changes over: Ready, registered, door open, and not on their way out, of either generation. The group builds one extra server at a time to keep it. Unset keeps no floor beyond one Ready server of the current generation.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>update.strategy</code></td><td>string (one of: RollingUpdate, WhenEmpty)</td><td align="center"></td><td><code>RollingUpdate</code></td><td>Strategy is how stale servers are replaced.</td></tr>

### status

Read by observers; the operator writes it and reads nothing back from it.

<div style="overflow-x: auto;"><table>
<thead><tr><th>Field</th><th>Type</th><th>Required</th><th>Default</th><th>Description</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><code>boostedReplicas</code></td><td>integer (int32)</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>BoostedReplicas is how much of this group&#x27;s current floor comes from ScaleBoost objects rather than from spec.scaling.minReplicas.<details><summary>more</summary>It exists because the likeliest failure of a boost is not a wrong number but an unexplained one: a group running four servers with a declared floor of one and nothing anywhere saying why. A person meeting that will edit the spec, which is the single thing that would not help -- the boost is a separate object and the spec is not where it lives.<br><br>Zero and present rather than absent, so that comparing two groups does not mean telling &quot;no boost&quot; apart from &quot;this operator is too old to say&quot;.</details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>changeover</code></td><td>string (one of: , Waiting, Begun, Deferred)</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Changeover is this group&#x27;s changeover as the network&#x27;s budget sees it; written by its own reconcile and read by its siblings&#x27;.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>conditions</code></td><td>array</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Conditions follow the standard Kubernetes condition contract.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>conditions[].lastTransitionTime</code></td><td>string (date-time)</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>lastTransitionTime is the last time the condition transitioned from one status to another. This should be when the underlying condition changed.  If that is not known, then using the time when the API field changed is acceptable.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>conditions[].message</code></td><td>string (length 0-32768)</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>message is a human readable message indicating details about the transition. This may be an empty string.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>conditions[].observedGeneration</code></td><td>integer (int64) (&gt;= 0)</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>observedGeneration represents the .metadata.generation that the condition was set based upon. For instance, if .metadata.generation is currently 12, but the .status.conditions[x].observedGeneration is 9, the condition is out of date with respect to the current state of the instance.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>conditions[].reason</code></td><td>string (length 1-1024; pattern <code>^[A-Za-z]([A-Za-z0-9_,:]*[A-Za-z0-9_])?$</code>)</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>reason contains a programmatic identifier indicating the reason for the condition&#x27;s last transition. Producers of specific condition types may define expected values and meanings for this field, and whether the values are considered a guaranteed API. The value should be a CamelCase string. This field may not be empty.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>conditions[].status</code></td><td>string (one of: True, False, Unknown)</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>status of the condition, one of True, False, Unknown.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>conditions[].type</code></td><td>string (length 0-316; pattern <code>^([a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9]*[a-z0-9])?(\.[a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9]*[a-z0-9])?)*/)?(([A-Za-z0-9][-A-Za-z0-9_.]*)?[A-Za-z0-9])$</code>)</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>type of condition in CamelCase or in foo.example.com/CamelCase.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>consecutiveFailures</code></td><td>integer (int32)</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>ConsecutiveFailures counts *rounds* in which at least one server failed to start, with no success since. One pass adds one however many servers it saw fail: counting servers would let a group with a floor of six spend its whole budget in a single round, because the scaler creates the shortfall in one pass. It lives on the CR rather than in the operator&#x27;s memory because a restart must not reset it, which would restart the create loop it exists to bound -- the opposite of the empty-since clock, where a reset delays a scale-down and so errs safely.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>failureStreakKey</code></td><td>string</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>FailureStreakKey identifies what the servers counted in consecutiveFailures started with: the desired pod hash, the configOverlay ConfigMap&#x27;s resourceVersion and the spawnery.cloud/retry annotation. The streak is reset when any of them moves, and by nothing else. Opaque; compare it, never parse it.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>freeSlots</code></td><td>integer (int32)</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>FreeSlots is the number of seats a proxy can send a player to right now: the free slots of servers that are Ready, in the proxies&#x27; routing tables, accepting joins, and rendered under the group&#x27;s current spec. It is the scaler&#x27;s input, published. A server that has closed its door for a running round contributes nothing here even while its own maxPlayers minus onlinePlayers is not zero.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>lastFailureAt</code></td><td>string (date-time)</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>LastFailureAt is the newest status.failedAt this group has counted. It is what makes the count idempotent across resyncs, and the instant the backoff window runs from.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>observedGeneration</code></td><td>integer (int64)</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>ObservedGeneration is the spec generation this status was computed from.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>onlinePlayers</code></td><td>integer (int32)</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>OnlinePlayers is the sum of players across all ready servers.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>phase</code></td><td>string</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Phase says whether players can join, and that is narrower than it sounds: Ready means the group&#x27;s *floor* is met -- spec.replicas for a persistent group, spec.scaling.minReplicas for an ephemeral one -- not that every server the scaler decided to run is up.<details><summary>more</summary>An ephemeral group scaled above its floor to cover spareSlots reports Ready as soon as the floor is covered, with the rest still starting. Compare readyReplicas against replicas to see that; both are printed columns for exactly this reason.<br><br>It is deliberately not &quot;every decided server is up&quot;. A group scaling up under load would then flip to Pending while thousands of players were connected, and a group whose cluster has no capacity left for its scaled target would sit at Pending forever while serving perfectly. Ready answering &quot;can somebody join&quot; is the more useful of the two.</details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>readyReplicas</code></td><td>integer (int32)</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>ReadyReplicas is the number of servers in phase Ready.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>replicas</code></td><td>integer (int32)</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Replicas is the number of Server objects owned by this group.</td></tr>
</tbody></table></div>


## ProxyGroup

**Scope:** Namespaced &nbsp;&nbsp; **Plural:** `proxygroups` &nbsp;&nbsp; **Short names:** `mcproxy`

ProxyGroup is the Velocity layer of a network.

### What `kubectl get` shows

<div style="overflow-x: auto;"><table>
<thead><tr><th>Column</th><th>Type</th><th>JSONPath</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td>Phase</td><td>string</td><td><code>.status.phase</code></td></tr>
<tr><td>Ready</td><td>integer</td><td><code>.status.readyReplicas</code></td></tr>
<tr><td>Address</td><td>string</td><td><code>.status.address</code></td></tr>
<tr><td>Players</td><td>integer</td><td><code>.status.connectedPlayers</code></td></tr>
<tr><td>Age</td><td>date</td><td><code>.metadata.creationTimestamp</code></td></tr>
</tbody></table></div>

### spec

ProxyGroupSpec describes the Velocity layer of a network.

<div style="overflow-x: auto;"><table>
<thead><tr><th>Field</th><th>Type</th><th>Required</th><th>Default</th><th>Description</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><code>attributes</code></td><td>map[string]string</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Attributes is what plugins are told about this group. See GroupAttributes: the operator carries it and acts on none of it.<details><summary>more</summary>It shapes no pod and is therefore not in the spec hash a server is replaced on -- the opposite of Env above. Editing it replaces nothing and restarts nothing; the next network picture simply carries the new value, which is what a description of a group should cost.</details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>config</code></td><td>object</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Config are the rendered Velocity settings.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>config.motd</code></td><td>string</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Motd is shown in the server list.<details><summary>more</summary>Editing it rolls the group&#x27;s proxies: the rendered config values are part of the pod digest, so the change reaches every proxy through a replacement at the group&#x27;s maxUnavailable pace rather than through a ConfigMap a running pod never re-reads.</details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>config.onlineMode</code></td><td>boolean</td><td align="center"></td><td><code>true</code></td><td>OnlineMode is whether the proxy authenticates players with Mojang.<details><summary>more</summary>Turning it off means the proxy stops authenticating anyone: any client may connect under any name, including the name of a player who has paid for the game and owns things on this network, and the network is only as protected as whatever sits in front of it. There is nothing further down that catches it — the backends run online-mode=false by design, because the proxy is the layer that was supposed to do this.<br><br>It is a field on the custom resource rather than something reachable through configOverlay so that turning it off is a visible edit to the object an operator reviews, not a line in a ConfigMap nobody reads.<br><br>This is the proxy&#x27;s own online-mode, not the backends&#x27; proxies.velocity.online-mode in paper-global.yml, which means &quot;trust what the proxy forwards&quot; and stays true either way: modern forwarding works the same whether the proxy authenticated the player or not.<br><br>Editing it rolls the group&#x27;s proxies, like Motd and PlayerLimit: the config values are part of the pod digest, so no proxy runs the old setting once the roll is through, and the roll starts on the edit.</details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>config.playerLimit</code></td><td>integer (int32) (&gt;= 1)</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>PlayerLimit is the network-wide player limit of one proxy.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>configOverlay</code></td><td>object</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>ConfigOverlay names a ConfigMap whose keys are configuration files to merge over the rendered defaults — &quot;server.properties&quot;, &quot;paper-global.yml&quot;, &quot;paper-world-defaults.yml&quot; or &quot;velocity.toml&quot;, in the target&#x27;s own dialect.<details><summary>more</summary>paper-world-defaults.yml is the one of those the operator writes only when an overlay names it. Nothing in it is operationally critical, so there is nothing to assert into it, and a file written empty on every start would overwrite whatever the server had filled in for itself. It is also the only route that file has: a mount cannot deliver it, because a mount anywhere under /data/config stops the server writing its own configuration and it never starts. See internal/podspec.ServerConfigDirPath.<br><br>It is a field of its own rather than a reserved name inside mounts, because mounts is documented as raw files for plugins and worlds and a name-based convention is invisible until someone picks that name by accident. It outranks the rendered defaults and is outranked by the operationally critical fields, which nothing can reach.<br><br>A key the receiving program does not declare is refused rather than written. Paper and Velocity both keep their own default for a key they do not read and write the stray one straight back out, so the rendered file goes on looking like the override took while the setting never applies -- which is the failure this refusal exists to prevent. The declared keys are taken from each program&#x27;s own default configuration, so a Paper or Velocity bump can refuse a legitimately new key until that file is captured again. server.properties is the exception: it has no such capture, so a mistyped key there is still only an unused one.</details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>configOverlay.name</code></td><td>string (length &gt;= 1)</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>Name of the referenced object.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>displayName</code></td><td>string (length 0-64)</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>DisplayName is what this group is called where a person reads it: a scoreboard, a chat message, a playtime key. A metadata.name is a DNS label -- lowercase, no spaces -- and a name people say out loud rarely is, so a plugin that shows &quot;Bingo-Team&quot; reads it from here and not from the object&#x27;s name.<details><summary>more</summary>The operator carries it and reads none of it, like Attributes below. Empty is not an error: a plugin then shows the group&#x27;s own name, and it is the plugin that makes that substitution rather than the operator, so that a picture with the field unset and a picture whose operator predates the field read the same.</details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>drain</code></td><td>object</td><td align="center"></td><td><code>{timeoutSeconds: 300}</code></td><td>Drain bounds how long existing sessions may run out on proxy replacement.<details><summary>more</summary>Editing it rolls the whole group, and that is worth knowing before an incident rather than during one. The value reaches the pod as terminationGracePeriodSeconds, so it is part of the rendered pod the group&#x27;s hash covers -- which means raising a drain timeout, the thing an operator does in the middle of an incident, adds a surge pod and a full replacement cycle on top of whatever prompted it.<br><br>Raising it while a drain is already in flight otherwise behaves: the marked pod keeps its mark, being now stale as well as draining, and the deadline is read from the current spec on every pass. So the edit is safe, just not free.</details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>drain.timeoutSeconds</code></td><td>integer (int32) (&gt;= 1)</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>TimeoutSeconds is the upper bound for the drain.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>env</code></td><td>array</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Env are extra environment variables for the proxy container, appended to the ones the operator sets. A name may not begin with ReservedEnvPrefix.<details><summary>more</summary>It is ServerGroupSpec.Env for a proxy, rule and reasoning unchanged, and JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS is the same seam: the Velocity entrypoint execs java with its own flag list too. It is in podspec.DesiredProxyHash for the same reason -- editing it rolls the group through the ordinary surge-1 path, and with the same limit: a valueFrom reference is digested, the value behind it is not.</details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>env[].name</code></td><td>string</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>Name of the environment variable. May consist of any printable ASCII characters except &#x27;=&#x27;.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>env[].value</code></td><td>string</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Variable references $(VAR_NAME) are expanded using the previously defined environment variables in the container and any service environment variables. If a variable cannot be resolved, the reference in the input string will be unchanged. Double $$ are reduced to a single $, which allows for escaping the $(VAR_NAME) syntax: i.e. &quot;$$(VAR_NAME)&quot; will produce the string literal &quot;$(VAR_NAME)&quot;. Escaped references will never be expanded, regardless of whether the variable exists or not. Defaults to &quot;&quot;.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>env[].valueFrom</code></td><td><a href="https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/api/core/v1#EnvVarSource">EnvVarSource</a> (Kubernetes, not expanded here)</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Source for the environment variable&#x27;s value. Cannot be used if value is not empty.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>expose</code></td><td>object</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>Expose makes the proxies reachable from outside the cluster.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>expose.clusterIP</code></td><td>object</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>ClusterIP configures type ClusterIP.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>expose.clusterIP.address</code></td><td>string (length &gt;= 1)</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>Address is what a player types.<details><summary>more</summary>Required, because the operator cannot learn it: it lives in an IngressRouteTCP, an HTTPRoute, a tunnel&#x27;s configuration or a DNS record — objects under APIs this operator does not read and cannot know are installed. Optional would make &quot;empty&quot; and &quot;forgotten&quot; the same state, which is the gap this strategy exists to close.<br><br>No port is required and none should usually be given: Minecraft clients default to 25565, so &quot;mc.paul.wtf&quot; is the whole of what a player types. Give &quot;host:port&quot; only when the entry point really is on another port.<br><br>Nothing checks that it resolves, that anything listens, or that it leads to this group&#x27;s Service. It is a sign on a door, not a test of the door.</details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>expose.hostPort</code></td><td>object</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>HostPort configures type HostPort.<details><summary>more</summary>It cannot coexist with Pod Security <code>baseline</code> or <code>restricted</code> in the same namespace: both disallow a container hostPort outright, so the API server refuses every pod of such a group and this operator reports the refusal on Degraded rather than ever admitting one. Against <code>restricted</code> the refusal reads:<br><br>violates PodSecurity &quot;restricted:latest&quot;: hostPort (container &quot;velocity&quot; uses hostPort 25577)<br><br>The remedy is a namespace of its own for the HostPort group, with a relaxed Pod Security label, separate from the restricted namespaces the rest of the network runs in.<br><br>That namespace is necessary and not sufficient. A hostPort that is admitted, ready and published in status.address can still be unreachable, because whether the port is open to the world is a host-firewall question rather than a Kubernetes one: a cluster-wide policy admitting a fixed list of ports from <code>world</code> drops this one while the pod serves perfectly. See docs/explanation/network-boundaries.md.</details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>expose.hostPort.port</code></td><td>integer (int32) (1-65535)</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>Port is bound on every node running a proxy pod. The kube-scheduler keeps at most one such pod per node, so replicas are capped by nodes.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>expose.loadBalancer</code></td><td>object</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>LoadBalancer configures type LoadBalancer.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>expose.loadBalancer.annotations</code></td><td>map[string]string</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Annotations are copied onto the Service, e.g. for MetalLB pool selection.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>expose.loadBalancer.externalTrafficPolicy</code></td><td>string</td><td align="center"></td><td><code>Local</code></td><td>ExternalTrafficPolicy defaults to Local so the client IP survives — bans and rate limits depend on it.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>expose.nodePort</code></td><td>object</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>NodePort configures type NodePort.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>expose.nodePort.port</code></td><td>integer (int32) (1-65535)</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>Port must lie inside the API server&#x27;s service-node-port-range.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>expose.type</code></td><td>string (one of: LoadBalancer, NodePort, HostPort, ClusterIP)</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>Type selects the strategy.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>extraFiles</code></td><td>object</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>ExtraFiles names a volume whose tree is copied into this group&#x27;s servers on every start. See ExtraFiles.<details><summary>more</summary>The claim&#x27;s contents are the truth on every start: a file the server rewrote at runtime is replaced by the claim&#x27;s version the next time the pod starts. A world placed in this claim is therefore overwritten on every start and does not belong here -- spec.storage and spec.mounts are what carry one.<br><br>Nothing about the contents reaches the pod hash, because the spec names a claim rather than describing what is in it. Changing a file replaces no running server; it reaches one on that server&#x27;s next start.</details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>extraFiles.claimName</code></td><td>string (length &gt;= 1)</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>ClaimName is a PersistentVolumeClaim in this object&#x27;s own namespace.<details><summary>more</summary>It must be ReadWriteMany, for the reason ExtraPlugins.ClaimName gives: every pod of a group mounts it, and a ReadWriteOnce claim would leave the second server Pending with a scheduling error naming volume affinity rather than the cause.</details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>extraPlugins</code></td><td>object</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>ExtraPlugins names a volume whose plugins and their configuration are copied into this group&#x27;s servers on every start. See ExtraPlugins.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>extraPlugins.claimName</code></td><td>string (length &gt;= 1)</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>ClaimName is a PersistentVolumeClaim in this object&#x27;s own namespace.<details><summary>more</summary>It must be ReadWriteMany. A ReadWriteOnce claim mounts on one node, so the second server of a group would sit Pending with a scheduling error naming volume affinity rather than the actual cause; the operator refuses it instead. That refusal also catches a single-replica group, for which ReadWriteOnce would in fact work -- the simpler rule was chosen because maxReplicas can be raised by an edit that has nothing to do with storage, and a group that worked until somebody scaled it is a worse failure than one that never started.</details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>image</code></td><td>string (length &gt;= 1)</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>Image is the Velocity base image. A digest reference is recommended.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>mounts</code></td><td>array</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Mounts are extra ConfigMap, Secret and PersistentVolumeClaim mounts.<details><summary>more</summary>It is ServerGroupSpec.Mounts for a proxy, and it is here because a network&#x27;s proxies may read the same shared asset directory its backends do, out of a template that targets both.</details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>mounts[].configMap</code></td><td><a href="https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/api/core/v1#ConfigMapVolumeSource">ConfigMapVolumeSource</a> (Kubernetes, not expanded here)</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>ConfigMap source.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>mounts[].mountPath</code></td><td>string (pattern <code>^/.*</code>)</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>MountPath is the absolute path inside the container.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>mounts[].name</code></td><td>string (length &gt;= 1)</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>Name of the volume inside the pod.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>mounts[].persistentVolumeClaim</code></td><td>object</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>PersistentVolumeClaim source. See MountClaim.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>mounts[].persistentVolumeClaim.claimName</code></td><td>string (length &gt;= 1)</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>ClaimName is a PersistentVolumeClaim in this object&#x27;s own namespace.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>mounts[].persistentVolumeClaim.writable</code></td><td>boolean</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Writable mounts the claim read-write. It defaults to false, and the field is spelled this way round -- Writable rather than ReadOnly -- so that the zero value is the safe one. An omitted field, a field somebody has not heard of, and a field lost in a hand-written manifest all land on read-only.<details><summary>more</summary>One group writing a volume that others read is the case this exists for: a generator filling a pool of worlds that game servers consume. Nothing here coordinates that. Two groups that both write the same claim get exactly what two processes writing one filesystem get, and the operator has no way to know which of them meant to.<br><br>It reaches the pod, so flipping it replaces the group&#x27;s servers.</details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>mounts[].secret</code></td><td><a href="https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/api/core/v1#SecretVolumeSource">SecretVolumeSource</a> (Kubernetes, not expanded here)</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Secret source.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>mounts[].subPath</code></td><td>string</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>SubPath mounts one file or one subdirectory of the source instead of the whole of it, so that MountPath can be a file.<details><summary>more</summary>Without it, a mount whose path names a file gets a *directory* there -- the source&#x27;s keys as separate files inside it. A server looking for /data/bukkit.yml then finds a directory called bukkit.yml, and what it reports is a parse error rather than anything about a mount. Landing a single file beside the ones the server writes itself is the case this exists for; there is no other way to do it.<br><br>**A ConfigMap or Secret mounted through subPath does not update.** Kubernetes refreshes a projected volume in place, and a subPath mount is a bind of one file out of it that the kubelet does not re-point. Editing the ConfigMap changes nothing in a running pod, and nothing reports that. Without subPath the file does update, eventually and without a restart -- which is a real difference and the reason this is a field somebody opts into rather than something inferred from the path looking like a file. Neither behaviour reaches the pod digest either way, so no edit to a ConfigMap&#x27;s contents rolls anything.</details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>networkRef</code></td><td>object</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>NetworkRef names the Network this group belongs to. Immutable.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>networkRef.name</code></td><td>string (length &gt;= 1)</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>Name of the referenced object.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>replicas</code></td><td>integer (int32) (&gt;= 1)</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>Replicas is the number of proxy pods.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>resources</code></td><td><a href="https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/api/core/v1#ResourceRequirements">ResourceRequirements</a> (Kubernetes, not expanded here)</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Resources overrides Network.spec.defaults.resources.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>routing</code></td><td>object</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>Routing configures the fallback groups.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>routing.fallbackGroups</code></td><td>array of string (at least 1 item(s))</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>FallbackGroups is the ordered try-list on join and on drain.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>scheduling</code></td><td>object</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Scheduling overrides Network.spec.defaults.scheduling.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>scheduling.affinity</code></td><td><a href="https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/api/core/v1#Affinity">Affinity</a> (Kubernetes, not expanded here)</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Affinity expresses scheduling preferences and constraints.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>scheduling.nodeSelector</code></td><td>map[string]string</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>NodeSelector restricts pods to nodes carrying all these labels.</td></tr>

## Server

**Scope:** Namespaced &nbsp;&nbsp; **Plural:** `servers` &nbsp;&nbsp; **Short names:** `mcsrv`

Server is a single running Minecraft server instance.

### What `kubectl get` shows

<thead><tr><th>Column</th><th>Type</th><th>JSONPath</th></tr></thead>

<tr><td>Group</td><td>string</td><td><code>.spec.groupRef.name</code></td></tr>

<tr><td>Registered</td><td>boolean</td><td><code>.status.registered</code></td></tr>
<tr><td>Age</td><td>date</td><td><code>.metadata.creationTimestamp</code></td></tr>
</tbody></table></div>

### spec

ServerSpec describes one running Minecraft server instance. It is created and owned by a ServerGroup and is not meant to be edited by hand.

<div style="overflow-x: auto;"><table>
<thead><tr><th>Field</th><th>Type</th><th>Required</th><th>Default</th><th>Description</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><code>groupGeneration</code></td><td>integer (int64)</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>GroupGeneration is the metadata.generation of the group at creation time. A server whose value is behind the group&#x27;s is stale.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>groupRef</code></td><td>object</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>GroupRef names the owning ServerGroup.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>groupRef.name</code></td><td>string (length &gt;= 1)</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>Name of the referenced object.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>key</code></td><td>string</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Key is the caller&#x27;s name for the world this member carries, and it is set for a member of an OnDemand group and for no other server.<details><summary>more</summary>It is here for the reason Ordinal is: a Server has to be able to say what kind of member it is without its group, and the Server controller reconstructs a synthetic group from this object alone when the real one is gone. An inference from Ordinal alone was exhaustive while there were two types; with three, a member with neither marker would read as ephemeral, which is the one answer that is wrong about its world.</details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>number</code></td><td>integer (int32) (&gt;= 0)</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Number is which of its group&#x27;s servers this is, counted the way a person counts: the second hub is 2. The group assigns it once, at creation, and it is given out again only after this server is gone.<details><summary>more</summary>Zero means nobody numbered this server: every server that was already running when this field arrived, and the ordinal-zero server of a persistent group, whose number is its ordinal. Nothing backfills them, and a reader showing this to a player falls back to the name it already has. That the two cases are indistinguishable is deliberate — a persistent server is referred to by the name that names its world, so falling back to that name loses nothing.<br><br>Not Ordinal, and the difference is what each one is for: that one is a persistent server&#x27;s identity, the thing its storage claim is named from, and its presence is read elsewhere as &quot;this server is persistent&quot;. This one is a label a player reads, and every server has one. A persistent server&#x27;s Number equals its Ordinal, so the number a person sees agrees with the name the server already has.</details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>ordinal</code></td><td>integer (int32) (&gt;= 0)</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Ordinal is the stable index of a persistent server. Unset for ephemeral servers, whose names carry a random suffix instead.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>podHash</code></td><td>string</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>PodHash is podspec.DesiredServerHash at the moment this server was created: a digest of everything the operator would render for it. The group compares it against a freshly computed one to decide whether this ordinal is running the current spec.<details><summary>more</summary>Empty means adopt, never stale. Every server that existed before this field did carries an empty value, and reading that as stale would restart every world in the installation on the first reconcile after an upgrade. The group stamps the current hash onto such a server and orders no takedown.</details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>retire</code></td><td>boolean</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>Retire asks this server to stop taking joins and empty out, without its players being moved. The ServerGroup controller sets it during a rolling update, and -- since the /cloud command -- an administrator can too, through the agent endpoint&#x27;s retire request rather than by editing this object. It is also the single signal for spec.update.maxUnavailable: a server counts against that budget while this is true, which is what tells a retirement apart from a drain a scale-down or a deletion started.<details><summary>more</summary>That second writer is why the controller&#x27;s own retireServer checks the flag before patching: it can now find a server already retiring for a reason it did not cause, and must treat that as done rather than as a state to correct.</details></td></tr>
</tbody></table></div>

<tr><td><code>startedAt</code></td><td>string (date-time)</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>StartedAt is when this server last began trying to become playable: the first pass that accepted it, then the pod creation, and then every entry into phase Starting. Do not change this back to pod-creation time.<details><summary>more</summary>The acceptance stamp is what gives a Server whose pod is never created a clock at all. Written only beside the pod, it left such a Server without one: nothing could fail it, so it sat in Pending occupying its group&#x27;s slot for as long as whatever refused the pod stood.</details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>storageResizeError</code></td><td>string</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>StorageResizeError names why this server&#x27;s claim has not grown to spec.storage.size, or is empty when it has (or there is nothing to grow). It covers both shapes a resize can fail in: a patch the API server&#x27;s own admission refuses synchronously, ordinarily because the claim&#x27;s storage class sets allowVolumeExpansion: false, and a resize admission accepted that a driver later fails, reported only on the claim itself through its ControllerResizeError or NodeResizeError condition.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>storageResizePending</code></td><td>boolean</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>StorageResizePending is true while this server&#x27;s claim carries the FileSystemResizePending condition: the CSI driver has grown the volume and needs the pod restarted before the filesystem follows. Most drivers expand online and never set it.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>wasRegistered</code></td><td>boolean</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>WasRegistered is true once this server has been registered with the proxies during the life of its current pod. A server that fell out of Ready is back in Starting but still has its players connected — deregistering stopped new joins, it did not move anyone — so the phase alone cannot tell us whether players are at risk.</td></tr>
</tbody></table></div>


## ScaleBoost

**Scope:** Namespaced &nbsp;&nbsp; **Plural:** `scaleboosts` &nbsp;&nbsp; **Short names:** `boost`

ScaleBoost is extra capacity for a group, for a while.<details><summary>more</summary>It exists as its own object rather than as a field on the group, and the reason is not tidiness. The operator has no write access to a ServerGroup&#x27;s spec -- its ClusterRole grants get, list and watch -- and on a GitOps-managed cluster that spec is owned by a file, so a floor the operator raised there would be reverted at the next reconciliation. An admin would type a command, watch the count rise, and find it back where the file has it. This object is the operator&#x27;s own, and nothing outside the cluster claims it.<br><br>It adds to the group&#x27;s floor and never to its ceiling. spec.scaling. maxReplicas still binds, because a ceiling is an instruction and a boost is the one thing here that a person might create in a hurry.<br><br>It has no status. There is nothing about a boost that the operator observes and the object does not already say: whether it is live is its expiry against the clock, and what it did is on the group it names, as status.boostedReplicas. A status here would be a second place to read one fact.</details>

### spec

ScaleBoostSpec is extra capacity for one group, for a while.

<div style="overflow-x: auto;"><table>
<thead><tr><th>Field</th><th>Type</th><th>Required</th><th>Default</th><th>Description</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><code>expiresAt</code></td><td>string (date-time)</td><td align="center"></td><td></td><td>ExpiresAt is when this boost stops counting.<details><summary>more</summary>Optional in the type and supplied by everything that creates one. A boost with none never expires, which is a real need -- a maintenance window somebody is watching -- and a real hazard: the boost from last weekend still running in March, with nobody left who remembers why the lobby has four servers. Whatever creates these gives them a default, and the type does not, because a type that invented a time would make an explicit &quot;forever&quot; impossible to write.</details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>groupRef</code></td><td>object</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>GroupRef names the ServerGroup this adds capacity to. Immutable in practice: nothing edits a boost, and moving one between groups would be two decisions wearing one object.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>groupRef.name</code></td><td>string (length &gt;= 1)</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>Name of the referenced object.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>replicas</code></td><td>integer (int32) (&gt;= 1)</td><td align="center">&#10003;</td><td></td><td>Replicas is how many servers to add to the group&#x27;s own floor.<details><summary>more</summary>Added, not set: two boosts on one group are two boosts, and a second does not replace a first. That is what makes &quot;somebody else already boosted this&quot; a non-event rather than a race.</details></td></tr>
</tbody></table></div>
